meta_desc: NCERT Class 12 Maths Exercise 7.8 solutions: evaluate definite integrals as the limit of a sum, with a free 8-question quiz to test your first principles.

quiz.title: Definite Integral as a Limit of a Sum Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the first-principles definition from Exercise 7.8 — the width h, the sum formulas, and evaluating integrals from the definition. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Definite integral as the limit of a sum (NCERT Exercise 7.8)

questions.q: In the definition ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x) dx = lim<sub>n→∞</sub> h[f(a) + f(a+h) + …], what does h equal?
questions.explanation: The interval [a, b] is cut into n equal strips, so each strip has width h = (b − a)/n.

questions.q: Evaluating ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> x dx as a limit of a sum gives what value?
questions.explanation: With a = 0, b = 1, h = 1/n, the sum is h(0 + h + 2h + …) = h²(0+1+…+(n−1)) = (1/n²)·n(n−1)/2 → 1/2.

questions.q: What is the value of ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>3</sup> x dx?
questions.explanation: Whether by the antiderivative x²/2 or the limit of a sum, the result is 9/2 − 1/2 = 4.

questions.q: Which formula for the sum of squares is needed to integrate x² from the definition?
questions.explanation: Σr² = 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. Its leading term n³/3 is what survives the limit.

questions.q: Evaluating ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> x² dx as a limit of a sum gives what value?
questions.explanation: With h = 2/n, the sum is h³(0² + 1² + … + (n−1)²) → (8/n³)·n³/3 = 8/3, matching [x³/3] from 0 to 2.

questions.q: As the number of strips n grows without bound, the strip width h behaves how?
questions.explanation: Since h = (b − a)/n and (b − a) is fixed, letting n → ∞ forces h → 0, so the rectangles shrink to the exact area.

questions.q: Finding a definite integral as a limit of a sum is another name for which approach?
questions.explanation: Exercise 7.8 evaluates integrals straight from the definition — first principles — without using any antiderivative shortcut.

questions.q: What is the value of ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> x² dx?
questions.explanation: With h = 1/n, the sum h³Σr² = (1/n³)·n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 → 2n³/(6n³) = 1/3, which equals [x³/3] from 0 to 1.

faq.q: What does Exercise 7.8 of Class 12 Maths cover?
faq.a: It asks you to evaluate definite integrals as the limit of a sum — the first-principles definition — instead of using antiderivatives. You split the interval into n equal strips of width h = (b − a)/n and take the limit as n tends to infinity.

faq.q: Which sum formulas do I need for these problems?
faq.a: The three standard results: Σ1 = n, Σr = n(n+1)/2, and Σr² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6. For most Exercise 7.8 questions the sum of the first n natural numbers and the sum of their squares are enough.

faq.q: Why do we bother with the limit of a sum when antiderivatives are faster?
faq.a: It shows where the definite integral actually comes from — the area under a curve as a limit of thin rectangles. Understanding this makes the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus meaningful rather than a rule to memorise, and it is regularly examined.

faq.q: What is a common mistake when evaluating these limits?
faq.a: Mixing up the sample points. Using left endpoints gives f(a), f(a+h), …, f(a+(n−1)h), so the sum runs to n−1, not n. Getting the endpoints and the limits of the summation right is where most marks are lost.
